definition: A paragon is a model of excellence — a person or thing so perfect of its kind that everything else is measured against it.

Renaissance jewelers kept a slab of fine-grained black stone — the paragone. Streak a ring across it and the color of the mark told you, on the spot, how pure the gold really was. To paragon something, in the old verb, was to put it to exactly that test, and the noun settled on whatever passes it. The trail behind the Italian likely leads to Greek parakonan, 'to sharpen against a whetstone,' but the root built nothing else in English — the touchstone is the whole family.
A paragon is a model of excellence — a person or thing so perfect of its kind that everything else is measured against it.
When the city audited its branch libraries, Elm Street emerged as the paragon: returns reshelved within the hour, waitlists cleared weekly, damaged spines mended and back in circulation within days.
By the second week the auditors had stopped scoring the other branches against the manual and started scoring them against Elm Street.
Paragon is the exact word because a paragon is not merely excellent — it becomes the standard itself, the case everything else of its kind is measured against.
Outstanding would only rank Elm Street near the top of the list; paragon captures the moment the branch stopped being a contestant and became the measuring stick.
Paragon is the measuring-stick word: name someone the paragon of a craft and you have made them the standard everyone else is scored against — a paragon of patience, a paragon of virtue.
Keep its neighbors straight: an exemplar is one good model among many, the ideal is perfection as a thought, and the paragon is the real one that comes closest.
It takes its quality in an of-phrase, and it always praises; there is no such thing as a minor paragon.

Every guide to America's old movie palaces ends up in the same seat: row F of the restored Orpheum in Marquette, under a ceiling of plaster stars.
Preservationists do not merely admire the Orpheum; they measure with it.
Grant applications for other theaters routinely include a page comparing their lobbies and sight lines to the Orpheum's.
The theater earned that place slowly.
Its restorers spent nine years matching the original gilding recipe and traced the 1927 seat fabric to a single mill in Ohio.
Critics who distrust the word 'perfect' still reach for it here, then catch themselves: the Orpheum is not perfection imagined, but the closest thing to it a visitor can actually sit inside.
That is what it means to call the building a paragon of restoration — the benchmark, real enough to sell tickets, that every other project is now judged against.
